chapters.summary: Council Member Jennifer Gutiérrez introduces herself as Chair of the Subcommittee on Early Childhood Education and welcomes everyone to the hearing on 2K in New York City.
chapters.title: Chair Gutiérrez welcomes attendees to 2K oversight hearing

utterances.speaker: Jennifer Gutiérrez
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: Jennifer Gutiérrez
utterances.text: Good afternoon, everyone.

utterances.speaker: Jennifer Gutiérrez
utterances.text: I'm Councilmember Jennifer Gutierrez, Chair of the Subcommittee on Early Childhood Education, and welcome to today's hearing on 2K in New York City.

chapters.summary: Gutiérrez notes that Governor Hochul and Mayor Mamdani announced free child care for two-year-olds through 2K, with 2,000 children already enrolled. She highlights that 5,700 families applied, demonstrating urgent need.
chapters.title: Chair Gutiérrez describes 2K launch and overwhelming demand

utterances.speaker: Jennifer Gutiérrez
utterances.text: Earlier this year, Governor Kathy Hochul and Mayor Zoran Mamdani announced a plan to deliver free child care for two-year-olds in New York City through a program called 2K.

utterances.speaker: Jennifer Gutiérrez
utterances.text: Within a few short months, the Mayor's Office of Child Care, along with the Department of Education, started to make good on that promise, with 2,000 of our littlest learners having started 2K just a few weeks ago.

utterances.speaker: Jennifer Gutiérrez
utterances.text: This is an amazing achievement as this program is saving New York City families enrolled in the program up to $26,000 per year per child in child care costs.

utterances.speaker: Jennifer Gutiérrez
utterances.text: When 2K applications opened this spring, over 5,700 families applied.

utterances.speaker: Jennifer Gutiérrez
utterances.text: That overwhelming demand tells a clear and urgent truth.

utterances.speaker: Jennifer Gutiérrez
utterances.text: New Yorkers need affordable child care and they need it now.

chapters.summary: Gutiérrez states that universal 2K cannot be achieved overnight and points to longstanding issues: pay inequities between community-based and public school educators, rising operating costs, and the need for dignified wages.
chapters.title: Chair Gutiérrez highlights pay inequities and provider challenges

utterances.speaker: Jennifer Gutiérrez
utterances.text: Unfortunately, we can't achieve a universal 2K program overnight, and there are longstanding issues with our current early childhood education system that need addressing.

utterances.speaker: Jennifer Gutiérrez
utterances.text: For starters, the inequities in early childhood educator salaries have persisted for far too long.

utterances.speaker: Jennifer Gutiérrez
utterances.text: Since the very first hearing of the subcommittee and at every hearing since, I've heard from early childhood education providers about the pay inequities between educators and community-based programs compared to those in New York City public schools,

utterances.speaker: Jennifer Gutiérrez
utterances.text: or about the challenges of rising costs of operating their business while salary raises have to take a back seat.

utterances.speaker: Jennifer Gutiérrez
utterances.text: These inequities need to be addressed as we look towards creating a stable and sustainable universal child care system.

utterances.speaker: Jennifer Gutiérrez
utterances.text: Early childhood educators are the heart of the early childhood education system and deserve to receive dignified wages for the important work that they do.

chapters.summary: Gutiérrez emphasizes that providers need reliable, on-time payments from the city, and that payment systems must be transparent and accessible so providers don't have to take out loans.
chapters.title: Chair Gutiérrez calls for on-time payments and transparency

utterances.speaker: Jennifer Gutiérrez
utterances.text: Early childhood education providers also need on-time reliable payments from the city for contracted work.

utterances.speaker: Jennifer Gutiérrez
utterances.text: Payment delays are unacceptable.

utterances.speaker: Jennifer Gutiérrez
utterances.text: Our payment systems need to be transparent, easy to navigate, and accessible.

utterances.speaker: Jennifer Gutiérrez
utterances.text: Providers shouldn't have to take out a loan to sustain their business month to month.

chapters.summary: Gutiérrez argues that expanding 2K must include pathways for home-based providers, noting that only those in family child care networks can currently participate in DOE contracted care.
chapters.title: Chair Gutiérrez advocates for including home-based providers

utterances.speaker: Jennifer Gutiérrez
utterances.text: Finally, as we think about expanding 2K, we must also think about expanding pathways for home-based providers to participate in the program.

utterances.speaker: Jennifer Gutiérrez
utterances.text: Too many home-based providers are left out of the current DOE system, as only those associated with family child care networks can participate in providing DOE contracted care.

utterances.speaker: Jennifer Gutiérrez
utterances.text: As the education system ages down, the city needs to be more inclusive of home-based providers.

utterances.speaker: Jennifer Gutiérrez
utterances.text: So today we...

chapters.title: Chair Gutiérrez outlines hearing goals and thanks attendees

utterances.speaker: Jennifer Gutiérrez
utterances.text: We'd like to look at what lessons the administration has learned so far from implementing 2K for this first school year and how the administration is planning to address longstanding issues in the early childhood education system.

utterances.speaker: Jennifer Gutiérrez
utterances.text: I want to thank members of the Early Childhood Education Subcommittee who joined.

utterances.speaker: Jennifer Gutiérrez
utterances.text: We've been joined by council members Kayla Santuoso.

utterances.speaker: Jennifer Gutiérrez
utterances.text: I'll make it up.

utterances.text: Council Members Gail Brewer and Education Chair Council Member Eric Dinowitz.

utterances.speaker: Jennifer Gutiérrez
utterances.text: I would also like to thank the staff of the Early Childhood Education Subcommittee, Julia Goldsmith-Pinkham, Katie Salina, Grace Amato, Andrew Lane-Lawless, and Margaret Barnsley, as well as my own staff, Frank Hulka and Helica Colon and

utterances.speaker: Jennifer Gutiérrez
utterances.text: Madeline, who just joined this week.

utterances.speaker: Jennifer Gutiérrez
utterances.text: And finally, thank you to everyone who has signed up to testify.

utterances.speaker: Jennifer Gutiérrez
utterances.text: We look forward to hearing from you.

chapters.summary: Emmy Liss, Executive Director of the Mayor's Office of Child Care and Early Childhood Education, introduces herself and her colleagues from NYC Public Schools, thanking the committee for the opportunity to testify on 2K.
chapters.title: Emmy Liss introduces herself and thanks committee

utterances.speaker: Emmy Liss
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Chair Gutierrez, Education Chair Dinowitz, members of the Subcommittee on Early Childhood Education, and other council members.

utterances.speaker: Emmy Liss
utterances.text: My name is Emmy Liss, and I am the Executive Director of the Mayor's Office of Child Care and Early Childhood Education.

utterances.speaker: Emmy Liss
utterances.text: I'm joined today by my colleagues from New York City Public Schools.

utterances.speaker: Emmy Liss
utterances.text: Thank you for giving us the opportunity to testify about the city's new 2K program, a critical component of our vision for universal child care.

chapters.summary: Liss describes Mayor Mamdani's vision for universal child care and the $1.2 billion state commitment, including $73 million for 2K's first year and $425 million for the second year to expand to 12,000 seats.
chapters.title: Liss outlines vision for universal child care and state funding

utterances.speaker: Emmy Liss
utterances.text: Mayor Mamdani ran for office on a vision of universal child care, a city in which every child under five has access to free, full-day, high-quality early care and education

utterances.speaker: Emmy Liss
utterances.text: in a range of culturally competent settings with caregivers and educators who are trained, respected, and fairly compensated.

utterances.speaker: Emmy Liss
utterances.text: On just day eight of this administration, the mayor stood with the governor as she committed over $1.2 billion to New York City to put us on a path to universal child care.

utterances.speaker: Emmy Liss
utterances.text: Within that $1.2 billion commitment was the funding to launch 2K, the city's first universal early care and education program for two-year-olds.

utterances.speaker: Emmy Liss
utterances.text: The governor committed $73 million for the program for the first year, with a goal of serving at least 2,000 children this fall.

utterances.speaker: Emmy Liss
utterances.text: and $425 million for the second year with a goal of expanding by 10,000 seats to serve a total of 12,000 children in fall 2027.

utterances.speaker: Emmy Liss
utterances.text: The mayor and governor have made the shared commitment that we will reach every two-year-old in New York City that wants to participate by the end of the mayor's first term in the fall of 2029.

utterances.speaker: Emmy Liss
utterances.text: We are committed to delivering 2K to all New Yorkers because of the tremendous benefit it will bring to children, families, educators, and our city.

chapters.summary: Liss explains that 90% of brain development occurs before age 5, parents spend an average of $26,000 on child care, and 2K will help families stay in the city and boost the local economy.
chapters.title: Liss details benefits of 2K for children, families, and economy

utterances.speaker: Emmy Liss
utterances.text: Children experience 90% of brain development before age 5 and a majority of it in their first few years of life.

utterances.speaker: Emmy Liss
utterances.text: Providing more children with high-quality early learning opportunities will set them up for a lifetime of academic and social-emotional success.

utterances.speaker: Emmy Liss
utterances.text: Parents currently spend an average of $26,000 for full-time child care for a two-year-old, though many families pay even more.

utterances.speaker: Emmy Liss
utterances.text: For parents, this can make it impossible to stay at a job they love and need to provide for their family because the math simply does not work.

utterances.speaker: Emmy Liss
utterances.text: For many, this leads to debt, tough trade-offs, or ultimately the decision to leave New York City.

utterances.speaker: Emmy Liss
utterances.text: Free 2K will make it easier for families to stay and raise their children here.

utterances.speaker: Emmy Liss
utterances.text: Because 2K will be offered in partnership with community-based child care programs and home-based providers, the program will bring resources to the work our educators and caregivers are already doing.

utterances.speaker: Emmy Liss
utterances.text: We have an opportunity, if we roll this program out in the right way, to support early childhood programs and educators as we do.

utterances.speaker: Emmy Liss
utterances.text: Ultimately, we believe 2K will bring significant economic return to our city, with more parents able to join the workforce, more families able to use their hard-earned resources in our local economy,

utterances.speaker: Emmy Liss
utterances.text: and more households with children able to stay in the city.

utterances.speaker: Emmy Liss
utterances.text: Despite the good return on investment, we are not doing this just for economic reasons, but more so because we believe that child care is and should be treated as a public good, and 2K is our first step toward delivering on that vision.

chapters.summary: Liss says 2K expanded geographically to meet full demand, selecting districts based on economic need, existing provider capacity, and geographic spread. She lists the five districts chosen for fall 2026.
chapters.title: Liss explains geographic expansion and district selection criteria

utterances.speaker: Emmy Liss
utterances.text: We made the decision to expand 2K geographically so that when we bring 2K to a new area, we can work to meet full demand from the outset.

utterances.speaker: Emmy Liss
utterances.text: This aligns to our value that care should be universal.

utterances.speaker: Emmy Liss
utterances.text: In selecting where to place the first 2,000 seats for fall 2026, we looked at a multitude of factors, including economic need among families and areas where lower-income families had less access to free or subsidized care already.

utterances.speaker: Emmy Liss
utterances.text: We also considered licensed child care provider capacity.

utterances.speaker: Emmy Liss
utterances.text: Given the short timeline for implementation, we wanted to ensure that whichever neighborhoods we selected would have the capacity to serve interested children.

utterances.speaker: Emmy Liss
utterances.text: Lastly, we considered geography to spread 2K across as many boroughs as possible.

utterances.speaker: Emmy Liss
utterances.text: The areas we selected for 2K for fall 2026 included School District 6 in Manhattan, which includes Washington Heights, Hamilton Heights, and Inwood.

utterances.speaker: Emmy Liss
utterances.text: School District 10 in the Bronx, which includes Fordham, Belmont, Norwood, Morris Heights, Van Cortlandt Village, and Kingsbridge.

utterances.speaker: Emmy Liss
utterances.text: Districts 18 and 23 in Brooklyn, which includes Canarsie, Remsen Village, Brownsville, and Ocean Hill.

utterances.speaker: Emmy Liss
utterances.text: And District 27 in Queens, which includes Ozone Park, South Ozone Park, Richmond Hill, Woodhaven, Howard Beach, and the Rockaways.

utterances.speaker: Emmy Liss
utterances.text: While we have not finalized yet where 2K will be offered in fall 2027, we have committed that

utterances.speaker: Emmy Liss
utterances.text: The 10,000-seat expansion will include School District 31, which encompasses all of Staten Island.

chapters.summary: Liss notes that 2K is offered in community-based centers and family child care programs, not public schools. The default model is full day, full year, with some school-day options.
chapters.title: Liss describes provider types and program models for 2K

utterances.speaker: Emmy Liss
utterances.text: After the first five districts were announced in March, the team at New York City Public Schools worked tirelessly to bring early care and education providers into the 2K program.

utterances.speaker: Emmy Liss
utterances.text: 2K is offered in community-based child care centers and licensed family child care programs.

utterances.speaker: Emmy Liss
utterances.text: There is no 2K in public school buildings.

utterances.speaker: Emmy Liss
utterances.text: The 2K sites are inclusive of providers who already contracted with the city to offer 3K and pre-K services, as well as new providers who applied to a request for information and were awarded new contracts to offer 2K.

utterances.speaker: Emmy Liss
utterances.text: The default model for 2K is full day, full year, recognizing that working families need full-time child care that maps to their schedules.

utterances.speaker: Emmy Liss
utterances.text: We also recognize that not all families have the same schedules or care needs, and so there are some 2K programs that operate on a school day in your calendar.

chapters.summary: Liss describes the all-of-government outreach effort, including advertising and a jingle contest. Over 5,700 applications were received for 2,000 seats; 99% of families received an offer to a listed program, 59% to their top choice.
chapters.title: Liss details application outreach and offer results

utterances.speaker: Emmy Liss
utterances.text: Families were able to apply for the first 2,000 2K seats in June, and we mounted an all-of-government effort to ensure that families knew about 2K, knew how to apply, and had the support to do so if needed.

utterances.speaker: Emmy Liss
utterances.text: The city and community partners were on the ground in communities providing application assistance to families.

utterances.speaker: Emmy Liss
utterances.text: We advertised in local and ethnic media, leveraged social and new media, posted ads in multiple languages on LinkNYC terminals and in high-traffic small businesses.

utterances.speaker: Emmy Liss
utterances.text: We hosted a 2K jingle contest with celebrity judges Cardi B and Lin-Manuel Miranda to bring attention to the program, and we ran a 2K for 2K race in Inwood.

utterances.speaker: Emmy Liss
utterances.text: We are grateful to the many council members who partnered with us on events and helped spread the word.

utterances.speaker: Emmy Liss
utterances.text: their communities.

utterances.speaker: Emmy Liss
utterances.text: In total, we received more than 5,700 applications for the first 2,000 2K seats.

utterances.speaker: Emmy Liss
utterances.text: This overwhelming demand demonstrates why we need to move with urgency to continue expanding access to care.

utterances.speaker: Emmy Liss
utterances.text: In August, we made just over 2,000 2K offers to families who had applied.

utterances.speaker: Emmy Liss
utterances.text: The majority of families who received a 2K offer were given an offer to one of their top choices.

utterances.speaker: Emmy Liss
utterances.text: 99% of families received an offer to a program choice that they had listed on their application.

utterances.speaker: Emmy Liss
utterances.text: And among applicants who received offers, 82% received an offer to one of their top three choices, and 59% received an offer to their top choice.

utterances.speaker: Emmy Liss
utterances.text: Families who did not receive an offer were automatically placed on wait lists for any programs they applied to and were also encouraged to explore other program options and add themselves to those wait lists as well.

utterances.speaker: Emmy Liss
utterances.text: Since August, we have also seen hundreds of additional families who did not originally apply to 2K add themselves to program wait lists.

chapters.summary: Liss notes that 2,002 two-year-olds started 2K on September 10th and that the city will take valuable lessons from year one as it expands.
chapters.title: Liss reflects on first day and lessons learned

utterances.speaker: Emmy Liss
utterances.text: On September 10th, the whole city was watching as our first 2,002-year-olds walked into their classrooms and programs to begin a year of learning, play, and growth.

utterances.speaker: Emmy Liss
utterances.text: There is much to learn from this first cohort of 2K children and providers.

utterances.speaker: Emmy Liss
utterances.text: We know that we will take valuable lessons from year one and apply them as we continue to expand and strengthen the program.

utterances.speaker: Emmy Liss
utterances.text: I will now turn it to my colleague and partner, Deputy Chancellor for Early Childhood Education, Erica Phillips, who will speak to how 2K is working on the ground and what's next.

chapters.summary: Erica Phillips, Deputy Chancellor for Early Childhood Education, introduces herself and thanks the committee for the opportunity to testify on 2K implementation.
chapters.title: Erica Phillips introduces herself and thanks committee

utterances.speaker: Erica Phillips
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: Erica Phillips
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Chair Gutierrez and Education Chair Dinowitz and the members of the Subcommittee on Early Childhood.

utterances.speaker: Erica Phillips
utterances.text: Thank you for the opportunity to testify today about New York City Public Schools implementation of 2K and our work to expand access to high quality, affordable early care and education for children and families across New York City.

chapters.summary: Phillips describes her personal connection as the daughter and granddaughter of early educators, and her 20+ years of experience, including at the National Association for Family Child Care and All Our Kin.
chapters.title: Phillips shares personal background in early childhood education

utterances.speaker: Erica Phillips
utterances.text: Early childhood education is deeply personal to me.

utterances.speaker: Erica Phillips
utterances.text: I'm the daughter and granddaughter of early educators and caregivers, and I've spent more than 20 years working to expand opportunities for young children, support families, and strengthen early childhood systems.

utterances.speaker: Erica Phillips
utterances.text: Before joining New York City Public Schools, I served as the executive director of the National Association for Family Child Care, and before that, I spent eight years at All Our Kin working closely with family child care educators here in New York City.

utterances.speaker: Erica Phillips
utterances.text: I bring those experiences with me to New York City public schools, along with a belief that has guided my work throughout my career.

utterances.speaker: Erica Phillips
utterances.text: Expanding access and ensuring quality must go hand in hand.

utterances.speaker: Erica Phillips
utterances.text: Families need affordable care they can count on.

utterances.speaker: Erica Phillips
utterances.text: Children deserve environments tailored to the ways that they learn and develop.

utterances.speaker: Erica Phillips
utterances.text: And our educators and providers need strong support systems behind them.

utterances.speaker: Erica Phillips
utterances.text: My focus is on building on the work already underway, enhancing the systems and partnerships that will continue to support the growth of 2K, while improving our early childhood system more broadly.

chapters.summary: Phillips explains that two-year-olds learn through play, exploration, and routines, and that 2K provides affordable, high-quality care that supports their development while giving families reliable care.
chapters.title: Phillips explains how 2K benefits children and families

utterances.speaker: Erica Phillips
utterances.text: 2K expands access to affordable child care while providing young children with nurturing, engaging environments during a critical period of their development.

utterances.speaker: Erica Phillips
utterances.text: For families,

utterances.speaker: Erica Phillips
utterances.text: It means greater access to high-quality, affordable care that supports their two-year-olds' learning and development while giving families care that they rely on.

utterances.speaker: Erica Phillips
utterances.text: Two-year-olds learn through play, exploration, relationships, and routines that support their development.

utterances.speaker: Erica Phillips
utterances.text: They build language through books, songs, and conversations.

utterances.speaker: Erica Phillips
utterances.text: They develop early problem-solving skills through hands-on experiences and learn to communicate their needs, build relationships with other children, and become increasingly independent.

utterances.speaker: Erica Phillips
utterances.text: Learning happens throughout the day.

utterances.speaker: Erica Phillips
utterances.text: Including through everyday interactions and routines that help children feel secure, build confidence, and develop strong relationships with the adults who care for them.

chapters.summary: Phillips explains that NYC's mixed delivery system builds on existing community-based and family child care capacity. About 60% of 2K seats are in home-based settings through family child care networks.
chapters.title: Phillips describes mixed delivery system and family child care role

utterances.speaker: Erica Phillips
utterances.text: New York City's mixed delivery system is central to how we are approaching the expansion of 2K.

utterances.speaker: Erica Phillips
utterances.text: It allows us to build on the capacity and expertise that already exists across community-based organizations and family child care programs while offering families meaningful choices in how and where their children receive care.

utterances.speaker: Erica Phillips
utterances.text: Family child care is a significant part of our 2K strategy, with approximately 60% of 2K seats offered in home-based settings through our family child care networks.

utterances.speaker: Erica Phillips
utterances.text: For two-year-olds in particular, family child care can offer continuity, close and consistent relationships with caregivers, mixed-age experience, and care that is responsive to the needs of both children and families.

utterances.speaker: Erica Phillips
utterances.text: I have spent much of my career working with family child care educators.

utterances.speaker: Erica Phillips
utterances.text: New York City and nationally.

utterances.speaker: Erica Phillips
utterances.text: And I know both the value they bring to an early childhood system and what it takes to support them well.

utterances.speaker: Erica Phillips
utterances.text: Our family child care networks play an important role in that work, connecting providers with instructional support, coaching, family services, and operational assistance while preserving the strengths of home-based care.

utterances.speaker: Erica Phillips
utterances.text: As we plan for the continued growth of 2K, we want to build on the strengths of our mixed delivery system and ensure that family child care and our community-based organizations remain a meaningful part of that growth.

utterances.speaker: Erica Phillips
utterances.text: That means continuing to engage with providers and with family child care networks as partners while ensuring that the additional supporting efforts we engage in reflect the realities of delivering high-quality care in home-based settings.

chapters.summary: Phillips acknowledges that contracting and payment delays created challenges for providers. The city provided interest-free bridge financing and is working to register all contracts and make payments.
chapters.title: Phillips addresses contracting and payment delays

utterances.speaker: Erica Phillips
utterances.text: Launching 2K on an accelerated timeline required significant coordination across New York City public schools, city agencies, and our provider partners.

utterances.speaker: Erica Phillips
utterances.text: In the months leading up to the start of the school year, teams worked closely with programs in respect to our site and our program readiness.

utterances.speaker: Erica Phillips
utterances.text: enrollment, contracting, budgets, and other operational requirements involved in bringing new 2K seats online.

utterances.speaker: Erica Phillips
utterances.text: We also know that contracting and payment delays created real challenges for some providers as they prepared to begin services.

utterances.speaker: Erica Phillips
utterances.text: The city took steps to help programs manage those immediate pressures while contracts and payments move forward, including providing access to interest-free bridge financing through the returnable grant.

utterances.speaker: Erica Phillips
utterances.text: Grant fund teams across New York City public schools and city government have continued to work to address outstanding contracting and payment issues.

utterances.speaker: Erica Phillips
utterances.text: We have made significant progress and we will continue to prioritize those efforts until all 2K contracts have been registered until all contracts have been registered.

utterances.speaker: Erica Phillips
utterances.text: We are also focused on supporting strong and consistent implementation across the mixed delivery system.

utterances.speaker: Erica Phillips
utterances.text: Our teams are in close contact with our programs and our family child care networks, providing ongoing support and responding quickly when financial, operational, or programmatic needs arise.

utterances.speaker: Erica Phillips
utterances.text: That close engagement allows us to identify challenges early, connect programs to the support that they need, and coordinate across New York City public schools and city agencies when issues require a broader response.

chapters.summary: Phillips says NYC Public Schools is hiring 200 additional employees across early childhood and other offices to support expansion, including instructional coaches, social workers, and contracting analysts.
chapters.title: Phillips outlines capacity building and hiring plans

utterances.speaker: Erica Phillips
utterances.text: As we support implementation this year, we are also preparing for the next phase of 2K.

utterances.speaker: Erica Phillips
utterances.text: The program launched this fall with 2,000 seats across five school districts and will grow to serve 12,000 children across all five boroughs in fall of 2027.

utterances.speaker: Erica Phillips
utterances.text: Expansion at this scale requires the capacity and infrastructure to support it.

utterances.speaker: Erica Phillips
utterances.text: That means improving how we enroll and connect families to programs, how we support providers and educators, and how we manage critical operational functions such as contracting, procurement, and payments.

utterances.speaker: Erica Phillips
utterances.text: Some of this work is specific to 2K, but

utterances.speaker: Erica Phillips
utterances.text: Much of this is about strengthening the systems that support early childhood programs more broadly.

utterances.speaker: Erica Phillips
utterances.text: To support that work, New York City Public Schools is hiring an additional 200 employees across early childhood and other agency offices.

utterances.speaker: Erica Phillips
utterances.text: Many of the systems our programs depend on go beyond the division.

utterances.speaker: Erica Phillips
utterances.text: And building this capacity will allow us to deepen our coordination, address longstanding operational challenges, and better support a growing early childhood system.

utterances.speaker: Erica Phillips
utterances.text: As we prepare for continued expansion, we need to make sure the systems behind 2K grow stronger along with the program.

utterances.speaker: Erica Phillips
utterances.text: We are not only preparing to serve more children,

utterances.speaker: Erica Phillips
utterances.text: We are building the capacity to connect families to those opportunities and support quality consistently across a much larger system.

chapters.summary: Phillips emphasizes that timely funding, clear communication, and operational support are critical for provider sustainability. She has begun visiting programs and speaking directly with providers.
chapters.title: Phillips discusses provider sustainability and partnerships

utterances.speaker: Erica Phillips
utterances.text: That work is closely connected to provider sustainability.

utterances.speaker: Erica Phillips
utterances.text: Our ability to expand 2K depends on a strong network of community-based organizations and family child care programs that can continue to deliver high-quality care for children and families.

utterances.speaker: Erica Phillips
utterances.text: The challenges with contracting and payments this year reinforce the importance of improving systems that providers rely on.

utterances.speaker: Erica Phillips
utterances.text: Timely and predictable funding is critical, but so are clear communication, early planning, consistent guidance, and operational processes that providers can navigate effectively.

utterances.speaker: Erica Phillips
utterances.text: We know there is work to do in these areas, and these efforts will be an important part of enhancing our early childhood system as we continue to work together.

utterances.speaker: Erica Phillips
utterances.text: continue to grow.

utterances.speaker: Erica Phillips
utterances.text: Partnerships with providers will be critical as we move forward.

utterances.speaker: Erica Phillips
utterances.text: They bring deep knowledge of the children and families they serve and have first-hand experience with how our policies and processes operate in practice.

utterances.speaker: Erica Phillips
utterances.text: I have begun visiting programs and speaking directly with providers.

utterances.speaker: Erica Phillips
utterances.text: And that engagement will be an important part of my work as we continue to strengthen our early childhood system.

utterances.speaker: Erica Phillips
utterances.text: As we expand, we also need to be thoughtful about where new capacity is needed and how it fits within the early childhood landscape, already serving families across the city.

utterances.speaker: Erica Phillips
utterances.text: Continued growth should broaden access for families while strengthening a strong and sustainable provider network that will undergird the early childhood system as a whole.

chapters.summary: Phillips states that expanding from 2,000 to 12,000 seats requires matching quality, capacity, and infrastructure. She looks forward to working with providers, families, and the council.
chapters.title: Phillips concludes with commitment to quality and partnerships

utterances.speaker: Erica Phillips
utterances.text: The launch of 2K represents a significant expansion of early care and education in New York City, and it's an important step towards the city's broader vision for universal child care.

utterances.speaker: Erica Phillips
utterances.text: As we grow from 2,000 seats this year to 12,000 next fall, our responsibility is to ensure that expansion is matched by the quality, capacity, trusting relationships, and infrastructure needed to support it.

utterances.speaker: Erica Phillips
utterances.text: For families, that means access to high-quality, affordable care that they can count on.

utterances.speaker: Erica Phillips
utterances.text: For providers, it means stronger and more reliable systems that allow them to focus on serving children and families.

utterances.speaker: Erica Phillips
utterances.text: And for New York City public schools, it means continuing to strengthen how we support a large and diverse early childhood system while maintaining a clear focus on quality and children's needs.

utterances.speaker: Erica Phillips
utterances.text: As we continue this work, I am excited about what 2K can mean for New York City's children and families, and I am deeply committed to ensuring that we build the systems and partnerships needed to deliver on that promise.

utterances.speaker: Erica Phillips
utterances.text: I look forward to working with our providers, families, city partners, and the council as we prepare for the next phase of expansion.

utterances.speaker: Erica Phillips
utterances.text: Thank you for the opportunity to testify, and I look forward to answering your questions.

utterances.speaker: Emmy Liss

utterances.speaker: Jennifer Gutiérrez
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.text: How many do you anticipate to be enrolled by the end of the year?

utterances.speaker: Emmy Liss

utterances.speaker: Emmy Liss
utterances.text: So those children were given a delayed start date.

utterances.speaker: Emmy Liss
utterances.text: So if your birthday was November 15th, you can start services immediately thereafter.

utterances.speaker: Emmy Liss
utterances.text: Children can start services in family child care settings in a 2K seat prior to two.

utterances.speaker: Emmy Liss

utterances.speaker: Jennifer Gutiérrez
utterances.text: How many emergent multilingual children are enrolled in 2K?

utterances.speaker: Emmy Liss
utterances.text: That's not data we have yet, again, as we don't yet have enrollment data finalized, but that will be among the many things we look at to understand who is participating in 2K.

utterances.speaker: Jennifer Gutiérrez
utterances.text: And I think you may have shared this at our hearing last week, but can you just remind us what are the languages available for instruction at the 2K sites?

utterances.speaker: Emmy Liss
utterances.text: So we do not have any formal dual language 2K programs.

utterances.speaker: Emmy Liss
utterances.text: That said, we know that particularly among our home-based providers, there are many educators serving in 2K programs who serve a language other than English.

utterances.speaker: Emmy Liss
utterances.text: particularly thinking about neighborhoods like Washington Heights.

utterances.speaker: Emmy Liss
utterances.text: We know there are many Spanish-speaking 2K providers and in other communities reflecting the languages that families in those communities speak.

utterances.speaker: Emmy Liss
utterances.text: And so that's something during the process when families were exploring programs, they were able to connect with providers and understand what their options might be.

utterances.speaker: Jennifer Gutiérrez
utterances.text: Thank you.

chapters.title: Chair Gutiérrez asks about priority for families

utterances.text: Curious on the priority taken for families.

utterances.speaker: Jennifer Gutiérrez
utterances.text: You mentioned, obviously, kids that lived in the five districts had a priority.

utterances.speaker: Jennifer Gutiérrez
utterances.text: Was there any other level of priority if they had siblings that already attended the center or the space?

utterances.speaker: Jennifer Gutiérrez
utterances.text: Any other?

utterances.speaker: Emmy Liss
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: Emmy Liss
utterances.text: So among the children who applied to 2K, similar to our other enrollment processes, families could list many applications on their program.

utterances.speaker: Emmy Liss
utterances.text: And then with it at.

utterances.speaker: Emmy Liss
utterances.text: For each individual program, families are sorted into priority groups based on whether they are a continuing student in that program.

utterances.speaker: Emmy Liss
utterances.text: So if they had been attending daycare at that site previously, if they have an older sibling enrolled into the program, and if they live in the district.

utterances.speaker: Emmy Liss
utterances.text: And so we worked through those different priority structures, and all of that was made publicly available to families so that they could understand whether they fit into one of those priority categories for a specific program.

chapters.title: Chair Gutiérrez asks about first choice percentages

utterances.speaker: Jennifer Gutiérrez
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: Jennifer Gutiérrez
utterances.text: Do you have data?

utterances.speaker: Jennifer Gutiérrez
utterances.text: It's just two questions.

utterances.speaker: Jennifer Gutiérrez
utterances.text: Just curious in the same way that we ask about, you know, parents'first choice.

utterances.speaker: Jennifer Gutiérrez
utterances.text: Can you share what percent of families received their first choice?

utterances.speaker: Jennifer Gutiérrez
utterances.text: choice of a 2K seat?

utterances.speaker: Emmy Liss
utterances.text: So 59% of families received their first, their top number one choice.

utterances.speaker: Emmy Liss
utterances.text: 83% received one of their top three choices.

utterances.speaker: Emmy Liss
utterances.text: And 99% of families received a program that was somewhere on their application.

utterances.speaker: Jennifer Gutiérrez
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: Jennifer Gutiérrez
utterances.text: Okay.

chapters.summary: Gutiérrez asks how many 2K seats are extended day vs school day. Liss says the majority are extended day and year, with final numbers to come with enrollment figures.
chapters.title: Chair Gutiérrez asks about extended day vs school day seats

utterances.speaker: Jennifer Gutiérrez
utterances.text: How many 2K seats are extended day and how many are school day?

utterances.speaker: Emmy Liss
utterances.text: The majority of our 2K seats are extended day and year.

utterances.speaker: Emmy Liss
utterances.text: We will have those final numbers when we have our enrollment figures.

utterances.speaker: Jennifer Gutiérrez

chapters.summary: Gutiérrez asks about the total budget for 2K. Liss says FY27 budget is $73 million from the state, and FY28 is projected at $425 million to serve 12,000 children.
chapters.title: Chair Gutiérrez asks about budget for FY27 and FY28

utterances.speaker: Jennifer Gutiérrez
utterances.text: I am going to ask a few more questions, and then I know we have a number of colleagues that have some questions, so then I'll come back.

utterances.speaker: Jennifer Gutiérrez
utterances.text: I wanted to ask a little bit about the budget.

utterances.speaker: Jennifer Gutiérrez
utterances.text: So let me just...

utterances.speaker: Jennifer Gutiérrez
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: Jennifer Gutiérrez
utterances.text: Can you share what the total budget for 2K and FY27, not including the smaller, the birth to two program?

utterances.speaker: Emmy Liss
utterances.text: The total budget for FY27 is $73 million.

utterances.speaker: Jennifer Gutiérrez
utterances.text: That's the total.

utterances.speaker: Jennifer Gutiérrez
utterances.text: And that's the exact amount that's been allocated for the current 2K program.

utterances.speaker: Emmy Liss
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: Jennifer Gutiérrez
utterances.text: For FY27 or FY27 and 28?

utterances.speaker: Emmy Liss
utterances.text: That is, that $73 million is for this fiscal year, also obviously maps to this school year.

utterances.speaker: Emmy Liss
utterances.text: That is the funding we received from the state to support the year one 2K launch.

utterances.speaker: Jennifer Gutiérrez
utterances.text: Year one, okay.

utterances.speaker: Emmy Liss
utterances.text: We are projecting that 2K for the 2027-2028 school year, fiscal year 28, that budget will grow to $425 million, which has similarly been committed to by the governor.

utterances.speaker: Jennifer Gutiérrez
utterances.text: And that is a proposed expansion of seats are included?

utterances.speaker: Emmy Liss
utterances.text: Yes, the $425 million will allow us to serve 12,000 children next year.

utterances.speaker: Emmy Liss
utterances.text: So our 2,002K seats that we will have continuity on and an additional 10,000 seats that we plan to expand to next year.

utterances.speaker: Jennifer Gutiérrez
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: Jennifer Gutiérrez
utterances.text: Does NYCPS, you all anticipate needing additional funding for this current fiscal year to fulfill the 2K program?

utterances.speaker: Erica Phillips
utterances.text: We anticipate that we will fully expend all of the funds for the budget and the $73 million for the current year.

utterances.speaker: Jennifer Gutiérrez
utterances.text: Okay, so there's no anticipated increase in the November plan for this year?

utterances.speaker: Emmy Liss
utterances.text: No, not at this time.

utterances.speaker: Jennifer Gutiérrez
utterances.text: Okay.

chapters.summary: Gutiérrez asks how provider costs are determined. Liss explains providers receive a cost per child based on program operating costs, with four flat rates for center-based and family child care, extended day vs school day.
chapters.title: Chair Gutiérrez asks about cost per provider and flat rates

utterances.speaker: Jennifer Gutiérrez
utterances.text: Can you quickly, and then I'll pass it to my colleagues, can you share a little bit about how you all determine the cost for each provider, essentially, like how you were able to dole out those dollars?

utterances.speaker: Emmy Liss
utterances.text: Yes, absolutely.

utterances.speaker: Emmy Liss
utterances.text: So every provider receives essentially a cost per child times the number of children who are in their program.

utterances.speaker: Emmy Liss
utterances.text: And the 2K funding structure, those cost per child amounts, were developed based on an analysis of program operating costs, our existing early childhood program models, staffing requirements, program hours, facility costs, and administrative costs.

utterances.speaker: Emmy Liss
utterances.text: We also looked at how 2K compares to 3K and pre-K in terms of sort of the structural funding cost.

utterances.speaker: Emmy Liss
utterances.text: So, for example, a 2K classroom is smaller in terms of the number of children than a 3K or pre-K classroom in order to maintain healthy and safe ratios.

utterances.speaker: Emmy Liss
utterances.text: And so, therefore, the cost per child is higher because your fixed costs of staff and facilities are the same.

utterances.speaker: Emmy Liss
utterances.text: We offered this year a sort of flat rate.

utterances.speaker: Emmy Liss
utterances.text: to providers.

utterances.speaker: Emmy Liss
utterances.text: There are four of them.

utterances.speaker: Emmy Liss
utterances.text: There is a rate for center-based providers offering an extended day and year, a rate for center-based providers offering a schools year in your program,

utterances.speaker: Emmy Liss
utterances.text: a rate for family child care providers offering an extended day, and the fourth is a rate for family child care providers offering a school day and year program.

utterances.speaker: Emmy Liss
utterances.text: We also did allow providers who may have demonstrably higher rent or significant other fixed costs that exceed that flat rate to, with evidence, bring that to New York City public schools.

utterances.speaker: Emmy Liss
utterances.text: Overall, this funding structure is really intended to support providers, strengthen the early childhood program across the city, and allow us to expand in a sustainable way.

chapters.summary: Gutiérrez asks how rates were communicated and if providers feel it's fair. Liss explains providers were awarded seats and rates, and teams work with them on budgets and invoicing.
chapters.title: Chair Gutiérrez asks about rate communication and provider feedback

utterances.speaker: Jennifer Gutiérrez
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: Jennifer Gutiérrez
utterances.text: And the flat rates, it sounds like they're broken up into kind of four categories and then depending on like the cost of rent, for example.

utterances.speaker: Emmy Liss
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: Jennifer Gutiérrez
utterances.text: Are those based on, are the flat rates based on kind of what is that determining factor besides the per student?

utterances.speaker: Jennifer Gutiérrez
utterances.text: Is there anything, is it a different flat rate for a provider in Inwood who's doing extended day in her home versus someone in the Bronx?

utterances.speaker: Emmy Liss
utterances.text: The extended, there is no variation by geography, but the extended day and year rate is higher than the school day and year rate, reflecting that those programs offer 10 hours a day, 260 days a year, versus our school day and year programs are 180 days,

utterances.speaker: Emmy Liss
utterances.text: six hours and 20 minutes.

utterances.speaker: Jennifer Gutiérrez
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: Jennifer Gutiérrez
utterances.text: And then the kind of how were those rights communicated to the providers, I guess?

utterances.speaker: Jennifer Gutiérrez
utterances.text: Do they feel like this is fair compensation?

utterances.speaker: Jennifer Gutiérrez
utterances.text: What can you share about those?

utterances.speaker: Jennifer Gutiérrez
utterances.text: Like that amount.

utterances.speaker: Emmy Liss
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: Emmy Liss
utterances.text: So at the time that providers, so for existing providers who already contracted with the city for 3K and pre-K, they were able to express interest in offering 2K through a survey where they demonstrated that they had the capacity to add two-year-olds to their program.

utterances.speaker: Emmy Liss
utterances.text: New providers who did not previously contract with the city.

utterances.speaker: Emmy Liss
utterances.text: Completed a request for information and went through multiple phases to demonstrate their readiness to offer 2K.

utterances.speaker: Emmy Liss
utterances.text: And then at the time that the city was ready to move forward with providers, they communicated the number of seats that that provider would be awarded based on their capacity and demand in their area, and then the rate that the city was offering for those seats.

utterances.speaker: Emmy Liss
utterances.text: And then the team at New York City Public Schools has worked with providers to complete their detailed budgets, make sure that they have costs allocated in all the right places.

utterances.speaker: Emmy Liss
utterances.text: And that's an area where the team continues to work closely with providers and make sure that they have what they need to be able to invoice for services over the course of the year.

utterances.text: I don't have the rates right in front of me, but we will get those to you.

utterances.text: I look forward to that.

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: You've got early language, you've got literacy, you've got school readiness.

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: And so how are you going to know if you're achieving these goals?

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: Obviously, with training like that, it would help a lot.

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: So I'm wondering about the training for the teachers and Robin Hood in particular.

chapters.summary: Phillips describes professional development partnerships with Robin Hood and Bank Street, and the use of Teaching Strategies Gold for authentic assessment. She notes qualifications for staff working with two-year-olds.
chapters.title: Phillips answers on professional development and assessment

utterances.speaker: Erica Phillips
utterances.text: Thank you for that question and for witnessing that.

utterances.speaker: Erica Phillips
utterances.text: Yes, we are working on a lot of different professional development for our teachers and for our staff within the division, for our educational leaders as we are expanding into 2K.

utterances.speaker: Erica Phillips
utterances.text: Caring for infants and toddlers is a skill set that we want to make sure that all of our educators have.

utterances.speaker: Erica Phillips
utterances.text: So we've worked with Robin Hood.

utterances.speaker: Erica Phillips
utterances.text: We have a new partnership with Bank Street, which might have been that event that you went to.

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: They were there also.

utterances.speaker: Erica Phillips
utterances.text: Right, that you went to.

utterances.speaker: Erica Phillips
utterances.text: And so they are providing professional development on the social-emotional.

utterances.speaker: Erica Phillips
utterances.text: learning of toddlers and making sure that our instructional coaches are working directly with our educators.

utterances.speaker: Erica Phillips
utterances.text: In terms of the assessment and how we're looking at this, we are using an authentic assessment tool called Teaching Strategies Gold, and we will be using that to assess

utterances.speaker: Erica Phillips
utterances.text: how that classroom is being ran and the type of experiences that the young children are receiving.

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: So the ones who are working now with the two-year-olds in those districts, they already, as teachers, have had some kind of training that would mirror what I saw or not yet?

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: Like, well, they picked maybe because they had the training.

utterances.speaker: Erica Phillips
utterances.text: Absolutely, yes.

utterances.speaker: Erica Phillips
utterances.text: So there are qualifications, including experience working with young children for all of the staff.

utterances.speaker: Erica Phillips
utterances.text: And we know that there are a lot more opportunities and places where we can provide support, particularly around working with children who might have developmental delays, supporting family engagement.

utterances.speaker: Erica Phillips
utterances.text: It's a bit of both.

chapters.summary: Brewer asks if children can continue to 3K in the same program and whether future expansion will include public school spaces. Liss says continuity priority exists if program offers 3K, and 2K will remain in community-based settings.
chapters.title: Brewer asks about 2K to 3K continuity and public school spaces

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: Okay, and then one more question would be, the chair asked about it also, but when you're in 2K, can you get into the same program with 3K?

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: How does that work?

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: And then, you know, will the next round out have public school spaces or will it still continue to be the nonprofit?

utterances.speaker: Emmy Liss
utterances.text: So children who are attending 2K, if that program also offers 3K, then yes, they would

utterances.speaker: Emmy Liss
utterances.text: receive a continuing student priority to stay at that program for next year?

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: We don't know how many have that or as opposed to have to reapply somewhere else.

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: We don't know yet.

utterances.speaker: Emmy Liss
utterances.text: We don't, you know, we have not yet confirmed all of the different programming and seats that everyone will be offering for next year, but certainly that's something we will look at.

utterances.speaker: Emmy Liss
utterances.text: Continuity of care is an important value we know for families, for providers, and we will be looking at that as we work with programs to confirm capacity for next year.

utterances.speaker: Emmy Liss
utterances.text: Our intention for the long foreseeable future is that 2K will be offered only in community-based settings and family child care homes.

utterances.speaker: Emmy Liss
utterances.text: We are not looking to place 2K in public schools.

chapters.summary: Brewer asks what the 200 new employees will do. Phillips says they include field staff, instructional coaches, social workers, inclusion specialists, and contracting analysts to speed payments.
chapters.title: Brewer asks about roles of 200 new staff

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: And one more question.

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: Where are those 200 people going to do?

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: The ones you mentioned.

utterances.speaker: Erica Phillips
utterances.text: It's a great question.

utterances.speaker: Erica Phillips
utterances.text: So for the additional staff, that includes many of our field staff who are working directly with the child care program.

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: Have they started or they're going to?

utterances.speaker: Erica Phillips
utterances.text: Yes, some have started.

utterances.speaker: Erica Phillips
utterances.text: So we have hired additional staff and are continuing to actively recruit and hire for those.

utterances.speaker: Erica Phillips
utterances.text: But we have our instructional coaches, our social workers, our inclusion specialists.

utterances.speaker: Erica Phillips
utterances.text: Additionally, on the contracting and payment side, we are bringing in additional analysts so that we can facilitate these payments going through in a faster manner.

chapters.summary: Brewer asks if the $425 million is state or city money. Liss says it is state money for the program, while the city funds infrastructure like the 228 new staff through its budget.
chapters.title: Brewer asks about $425M funding source

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: Last question, the 425, does that include just state money or next year do you need city money?

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: You mentioned this year just state.

utterances.speaker: Emmy Liss
utterances.text: The $425 million is just the state money, and that is the funding.

utterances.speaker: Emmy Liss
utterances.text: for us to operationalize the program.

utterances.speaker: Emmy Liss
utterances.text: So that is the per child cost to run the program.

utterances.speaker: Emmy Liss
utterances.text: The cost that the city has incurred and will continue to support are, for example, the 228 staff who we are bringing on, those were funded through the preliminary and executive budget last year.

utterances.speaker: Emmy Liss
utterances.text: So the city is making investments to make sure we have the infrastructure to support the program.

utterances.speaker: Emmy Liss
utterances.text: And then the program itself is fully funded by those state dollars.

utterances.speaker: Erica Phillips
utterances.text: Thank you, Madam Chair.

utterances.speaker: Jennifer Gutiérrez
utterances.text: Next we have Councilmember, did I skip some?

utterances.speaker: Jennifer Gutiérrez
utterances.text: Oh, no, Councilmember Riley and then Sensuoso.

utterances.speaker: Jennifer Gutiérrez
utterances.text: And then Councilmember Joseph.

chapters.summary: Riley thanks the witnesses and asks how many of the 200 additional employees are dedicated to 2K vs. contracting and payments. Phillips says more are on instructional side, with a smaller but significant investment in operations and finance.
chapters.title: Council Member Riley thanks witnesses and asks about staff breakdown

utterances.speaker: Kevin C. Riley
utterances.text: Thank you, Chair.

utterances.speaker: Kevin C. Riley
utterances.text: Thank you so much for testifying.

utterances.speaker: Kevin C. Riley
utterances.text: And as a dad, I'm really, really excited about this program.

utterances.speaker: Kevin C. Riley
utterances.text: I think within our office, we get a lot of families that are looking for child care providers.

utterances.speaker: Kevin C. Riley
utterances.text: Child care is causing a lot of, you know, unintentional consequences for families who are trying to take care of their families and stick in an affordable New York.

utterances.speaker: Kevin C. Riley
utterances.text: So with that being said, I just want to ask questions.

utterances.speaker: Kevin C. Riley
utterances.text: You mentioned 200 additional employees to support the expansion.

utterances.speaker: Kevin C. Riley
utterances.text: Can you...

utterances.speaker: Kevin C. Riley
utterances.text: Name how many of those positions are specifically dedicated to the 2K program and how many are dedicated to contracting, procurement, or even providing payments.

utterances.speaker: Erica Phillips
utterances.text: Great.

utterances.speaker: Erica Phillips
utterances.text: The breakdowns that we're looking at across all of those places, we have more positions that are on the instructional side, so the instructional coaches, the social workers, and the inclusion specialists.

utterances.speaker: Erica Phillips
utterances.text: And it's a relatively smaller proportion, but still a significant investment in our operations and our finance staff.

utterances.speaker: Kevin C. Riley
utterances.text: Okay.

chapters.summary: Riley asks if there are enough qualified family child care providers and CBOs to support expansion from 2,000 to 12,000. Phillips says they are working with networks and feel confident there is capacity.
chapters.title: Riley asks about provider capacity for expansion

utterances.speaker: Kevin C. Riley
utterances.text: Do we currently have enough qualified family child care providers and community-based organizations to support an expansion from 2,000 to 12,000?

utterances.speaker: Erica Phillips
utterances.text: So we are working with our family child care networks and working with them to figure out what...

utterances.speaker: Erica Phillips
utterances.text: Providers are in their network, what their ability is to expand to care for more children.

utterances.speaker: Erica Phillips
utterances.text: So those are active conversations we're having.

utterances.speaker: Erica Phillips
utterances.text: And as we have more details in terms of where the seats will be needed, what the family need is, but we do feel confident that in the community, there are providers and seats that we're able to accommodate the expansion.

utterances.speaker: Kevin C. Riley
utterances.text: Okay.

chapters.summary: Riley asks what gives confidence that systems can handle a six-fold increase given current contracting and payment challenges. Liss acknowledges delays are unacceptable and cites procurement reform and additional staff.
chapters.title: Riley asks about confidence in handling six-fold increase

utterances.speaker: Kevin C. Riley
utterances.text: Proposing going from 2,000 seats to 12,000 seats in fall 2027, what gives you the confidence that the systems that are currently experiencing contracting and payment challenges will be able to successfully handle a six-fold increase in enrollment?

utterances.speaker: Emmy Liss
utterances.text: So I'm happy to start, and then I'll pass to my colleague.

utterances.speaker: Emmy Liss
utterances.text: But, you know, I think some of the payment and contracting delays that we saw this year, you know, as the mayor has said publicly, are unacceptable and do not represent the way that we as a city believe that we should be working hand-in-hand with our providers.

utterances.speaker: Emmy Liss
utterances.text: So our focus over the last couple months has been both to ensure that every provider had what they needed, that we were working quickly to register contracts and issue interest-free loans for providers who needed funding in the interim.

utterances.speaker: Emmy Liss
utterances.text: And at the same time, we are building new systems, rebuilding the sort of human capital and systems infrastructure to support this growth.

utterances.speaker: Emmy Liss
utterances.text: So the administration has committed to significant procurement reform, increased transparency for providers, and increased timeliness in the processing.

utterances.speaker: Emmy Liss
utterances.text: And then many of the staff that Deputy Chancellor Phillips has referenced to are coming on board will allow us to ensure more timely contracting and payment actions.

utterances.speaker: Emmy Liss
utterances.text: And so with all of that and the administration's laser focus on expanding, but expanding in a way that supports providers, we do feel confident about reaching the 12,000 seats.

utterances.speaker: Kevin C. Riley
utterances.text: Okay.

chapters.summary: Riley asks about the thought process for not having 2K in traditional school settings. Liss explains community-based centers and family child care are better suited for two-year-olds, and the city is honoring that expertise.
chapters.title: Riley asks about transition from home to school settings

utterances.speaker: Kevin C. Riley
utterances.text: And lastly, transitioning from in-home care to in-school care can be a little bit challenging for parents.

utterances.speaker: Kevin C. Riley
utterances.text: I could attest my son just went to pre-K, and it was really a challenge to get him from not being attached to his mother every time she's dropping him off.

utterances.speaker: Kevin C. Riley
utterances.text: So can you just explain?

utterances.speaker: Kevin C. Riley
utterances.text: explain the thought process in not having 2K inside of a traditional school setting, just on the record.

utterances.speaker: Emmy Liss
utterances.text: So when we look at where families with two-year-olds often choose to send their children for care, where we see the environments that

utterances.speaker: Emmy Liss
utterances.text: educators are trained and ready to welcome toddlers, those are our community-based centers and our family child care programs.

utterances.speaker: Emmy Liss
utterances.text: Those are spaces that environmentally are right for two-year-olds, where we have educators who have been working with toddlers for years and years and have gone through the training and experience to be able to serve them well.

utterances.speaker: Emmy Liss
utterances.text: And so we've really focused on expanding 2K in those settings because that is where toddlers in New York City are cared for today.

utterances.speaker: Emmy Liss
utterances.text: What we are doing essentially is saying rather than families pay out of pocket for that care, the city is stepping in to cover the cost of care, but we want to honor the expertise in those early childhood settings.

utterances.speaker: Kevin C. Riley
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: Erica Phillips
utterances.text: And out.

utterances.speaker: Kevin C. Riley
utterances.text: She said the state is covering it now.

utterances.speaker: Erica Phillips
utterances.text: I would just add on that as we're approaching the end of the year, we will be very intentional with having either pre-K or kindergarten information sessions so that families are able to get exposure to what the new program is.

utterances.speaker: Erica Phillips
utterances.text: We're working very closely with our school-based colleagues to really support the transition.

utterances.speaker: Kevin C. Riley
utterances.text: Yeah, and I think that's a great idea, just having some form of a blueprint for a parent that after their child has been in a home care provider system,

utterances.speaker: Kevin C. Riley
utterances.text: them into a traditional school setting will be extremely helpful.

utterances.speaker: Kevin C. Riley
utterances.text: Great work.

utterances.speaker: Kevin C. Riley
utterances.text: I'm looking forward to this expansion.

utterances.speaker: Kevin C. Riley
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: Kevin C. Riley
utterances.text: Thank you, Chair.

utterances.speaker: Jennifer Gutiérrez
utterances.text: 2K's number one fan right here, Councilmember Riley.

utterances.speaker: Jennifer Gutiérrez
utterances.text: Okay, thank you for your questions.

utterances.speaker: Jennifer Gutiérrez
utterances.text: Next up, we have Councilmember Santos-Wosso, Councilmember Joseph, and Councilmember Felder.

chapters.summary: Santosuosso asks if future 2K seats will remain full day, full year. Liss says full day, full year is the default, with options for school day based on community need.
chapters.title: Council Member Santosuosso asks about full day/year plan

utterances.speaker: Kayla Santosuosso
utterances.text: Councilmember Santis-Woso, 2K's future number one fan, hopefully.

utterances.speaker: Kayla Santosuosso
utterances.text: Thank you both for your testimony and for your work.

utterances.speaker: Kayla Santosuosso
utterances.text: I hope I have quick questions.

utterances.speaker: Kayla Santosuosso
utterances.text: First, for future 2K seats, so starting next year and beyond, is the plan still full day, full year?

utterances.speaker: Emmy Liss
utterances.text: Our plan is to continue with full day, full year as the default model, but with the option for providers based on their community need to opt into a school day and year program if that better fits their community.

utterances.speaker: Kayla Santosuosso
utterances.text: And I'm sorry if you said this and I didn't write it down.

utterances.speaker: Kayla Santosuosso
utterances.text: What percentage was full day, full year and what percentage was school?

utterances.speaker: Emmy Liss
utterances.text: The majority are full day, full year.

utterances.speaker: Emmy Liss
utterances.text: We'll have those final figures when we release the data.

utterances.speaker: Kayla Santosuosso
utterances.text: Okay, you did say that.

utterances.speaker: Kayla Santosuosso
utterances.text: I'm sorry about that.

chapters.summary: Santosuosso asks if the plan is to make 2K available to all two-year-olds after next year. Phillips says they have stated 12,000 for next year and are setting targets toward universal access by 2029.
chapters.title: Santosuosso asks about future availability for all two-year-olds

utterances.speaker: Kayla Santosuosso
utterances.text: Is the plan to make it available to all two-year-olds in the years after next year?

utterances.speaker: Kayla Santosuosso
utterances.text: Or how many, rather, how many two-year-olds do you anticipate?

utterances.speaker: Kayla Santosuosso
utterances.text: Not this coming next year.

utterances.speaker: Erica Phillips
utterances.text: Yes, so we've stated the 12,000 for next year, and with the goal of by 2029 having access for all two-year-olds, we're in the process of setting the specific targets.

utterances.speaker: Erica Phillips
utterances.text: Okay.

chapters.summary: Santosuosso asks when the next expansion neighborhoods will be announced. Liss says very soon, and the council will be briefed before public announcement.
chapters.title: Santosuosso asks when next year's neighborhoods will be announced

utterances.speaker: Kayla Santosuosso
utterances.text: When will you announce the neighborhoods?

utterances.speaker: Kayla Santosuosso
utterances.text: next year?

utterances.speaker: Emmy Liss
utterances.text: Very soon.

utterances.speaker: Emmy Liss
utterances.text: We are working towards finalizing that information because we know that families and providers are eager to be able to plan.

utterances.speaker: Emmy Liss
utterances.text: And we will, of course, brief the council subcommittee before that information is public.

utterances.speaker: Kayla Santosuosso
utterances.text: That wasn't a selfish question, by the way.

utterances.speaker: Kayla Santosuosso
utterances.text: She won't be eligible until the following year.

utterances.speaker: Kayla Santosuosso
utterances.text: So it's, you know, I'm just saying it's not just me.

chapters.summary: Santosuosso asks how waitlists will roll into next year's applications. Liss explains program-specific waitlists remain open year-round, and children eligible for 2K this year will be eligible for 3K next year.
chapters.title: Santosuosso asks about waitlist rollover to next year

utterances.speaker: Kayla Santosuosso
utterances.text: You mentioned that there was a wait list, I believe.

utterances.speaker: Kayla Santosuosso
utterances.text: And so how are you going to roll the wait list into next year's applications?

utterances.speaker: Kayla Santosuosso
utterances.text: What's the plan there?

utterances.speaker: Emmy Liss
utterances.text: So families who applied to 2K were added to the wait list under a few different circumstances.

utterances.speaker: Emmy Liss
utterances.text: And they are program-specific wait lists similar to 3K and pre-K.

utterances.speaker: Emmy Liss
utterances.text: So if you're a family who applied to 2K and you got your fourth choice on your application, you were automatically placed on the wait list for your first, second, and third choices.

utterances.speaker: Emmy Liss
utterances.text: If you applied to 2K and you did not get an offer at all, unfortunately, you were automatically placed on the wait list for every program you applied to.

utterances.speaker: Emmy Liss
utterances.text: And additionally, families who've subsequently sort of expressed interest in 2K can do so by adding themselves to program wait lists.

utterances.speaker: Emmy Liss
utterances.text: Those wait lists will remain open year round.

utterances.speaker: Emmy Liss
utterances.text: So as a program has a vacancy, they go to that wait list and they can call through families in the order they are on the wait list to offer them a spot on the spot.

utterances.speaker: Emmy Liss
utterances.text: For next year, the children who were eligible for 2K this year will all be eligible for 3K next year.

utterances.speaker: Emmy Liss
utterances.text: And 3K as a full universal program, we can accommodate all.

utterances.speaker: Emmy Liss
utterances.text: children who apply.

utterances.speaker: Emmy Liss
utterances.text: So all of those families will be able to get a 3K seat next year.

utterances.speaker: Kayla Santosuosso
utterances.text: Okay.

chapters.summary: Santosuosso asks about the mix of single-location vs multi-location providers and how many were existing vs new. Liss says they have a diverse mix, with majority previously contracting for 3K and pre-K.
chapters.title: Santosuosso asks about provider size and existing vs new contracts

utterances.speaker: Kayla Santosuosso
utterances.text: I'm curious about the size of the providers that were contracted this year.

utterances.speaker: Kayla Santosuosso
utterances.text: So do you have data around how many are single location providers versus a larger provider that might have multiple locations?

utterances.speaker: Emmy Liss
utterances.text: I don't know that we have that data yet available, but we do have a really diverse mix of providers.

utterances.speaker: Emmy Liss
utterances.text: We have, as you heard, many, many home-based providers who may be serving just a couple of 2K children alongside their other mixed-age enrollments.

utterances.speaker: Emmy Liss
utterances.text: And then we have single-site providers, independent organizations who are serving a classroom or two of 2K.

utterances.speaker: Emmy Liss
utterances.text: And then we do have larger providers who have multiple locations across the city who are serving 2K children in the locations inside the districts.

utterances.speaker: Kayla Santosuosso
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: Kayla Santosuosso
utterances.text: And so do you have the data around how many were existing, sorry, had existing contracts with the city versus brand new providers via the 2K program?

utterances.speaker: Emmy Liss
utterances.text: The majority of providers were previously working with the city to offer 3K and pre-K.

utterances.speaker: Emmy Liss
utterances.text: We did see a smaller number of providers who opted through the RFI to newly contract with the city.

utterances.speaker: Kayla Santosuosso
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: Kayla Santosuosso
utterances.text: I would love to see data as far as how many seats were in multiple network, multiple providers, home-based.

utterances.speaker: Kayla Santosuosso
utterances.text: center-based, et cetera, as a breakdown when possible.

utterances.speaker: Kayla Santosuosso
utterances.text: But I know you said November for that, right?

utterances.speaker: Emmy Liss
utterances.text: Yes, that's when we'll have preliminary enrollment data to share.

utterances.speaker: Kayla Santosuosso
utterances.text: Okay.

chapters.summary: Santosuosso asks why Staten Island was not included this year. Liss explains limited seats and the need for sufficient provider readiness, and notes they added 3K seats on Staten Island and plan to bring 2K next year.
chapters.title: Santosuosso asks about Staten Island exclusion

utterances.speaker: Kayla Santosuosso
utterances.text: Can you speak to the decision this year to not include Staten Island?

utterances.speaker: Emmy Liss
utterances.text: We were obviously limited with only 2,000 seats to where we could go.

utterances.speaker: Emmy Liss
utterances.text: And when selecting districts, our goal was to be able to serve as many children as possible in each of those districts so that we could really fully meet demand.

utterances.speaker: Emmy Liss
utterances.text: With Staten Island being one school district for the entire borough and with our relatively limited timeline to roll out 2K this year, we

utterances.speaker: Emmy Liss
utterances.text: wanted to make sure that we had sufficient provider readiness and felt we needed more time to be able to roll out to Staten Island in a way where we could really serve all families.

utterances.speaker: Emmy Liss
utterances.text: We also saw this year that we had continued unmet 3K demand on Staten Island, and that had been a real persistent challenge for families in certain parts of the island.

utterances.speaker: Emmy Liss
utterances.text: So in addition to our 2K expansion for this fall, we also added more than 2,000 new 3K seats across certain priority zip codes, which included significant parts of Staten Island.

utterances.speaker: Emmy Liss
utterances.text: And with that investment in capacity, we feel more ready to bring 2K to Staten Island next year.

utterances.speaker: Kayla Santosuosso
utterances.text: Kara, could I just have one more question, and then I will get out of your hair?

chapters.summary: Santosuosso raises concerns about DOH permitting delays holding up payments. Liss acknowledges the issue and says the Mayor's Office of Child Care is coordinating across agencies and monitoring DOH capacity.
chapters.title: Santosuosso asks about DOH permitting and agency coordination

utterances.speaker: Kayla Santosuosso
utterances.text: Okay, I guess when we're talking about additional staff, and I don't know if you share this perspective, but it does feel like some of the payments and the permitting get held up in agencies that are not DOE, for instance, within DOH.

utterances.speaker: Kayla Santosuosso
utterances.text: And so I'm wondering if there's a plan moving forward to not only boost the capacity of DOE in order to do these payments and to administer these contracts effectively, but also in the organizations that are part of the permitting process.

utterances.speaker: Kayla Santosuosso
utterances.text: EOH specifically.

utterances.speaker: Emmy Liss
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: Emmy Liss
utterances.text: So a big part of the function of my office, the Mayor's Office of Child Care, is to make sure that we are coordinating across all of the different agencies that touch child care so that we can ensure a more seamless experience for providers.

utterances.speaker: Emmy Liss
utterances.text: So a big part of our focus this year has been on just enhancing that coordination, making processes easier for providers, including with the launch of our permitting portal earlier this year, which we had the chance to demo for the subcommittee.

utterances.speaker: Emmy Liss
utterances.text: We did assess staffing needs at the Department of Health and made sure they had sufficient capacity to inspect sites, to complete background checks for staff.

utterances.speaker: Emmy Liss
utterances.text: We had a relatively small number of programs coming into 2K that had new permits this year, just because given the short timeline, we primarily focused on bringing in providers who were already permitted to serve two-year-olds.

utterances.speaker: Emmy Liss
utterances.text: As we expand further, we do anticipate...

utterances.speaker: Emmy Liss
utterances.text: Bringing programs in that are opening for the first time or doing some sort of permanent amendment to add 2K capacity.

utterances.speaker: Emmy Liss
utterances.text: And so we will be closely monitoring the Department of Health's capacity as well as our other agency partners.

utterances.speaker: Kayla Santosuosso
utterances.text: Yeah, I only say it because I had two, they weren't 2K programs, obviously, they were preschools, but I had two preschools that were completely held up by DOH with

utterances.speaker: Kayla Santosuosso
utterances.text: re-permitting, re-inspection issues that ultimately they couldn't get their payments because they weren't cleared from DOH.

utterances.speaker: Kayla Santosuosso
